title: Debugging Deployment-Specific Problems
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of debugging deployment-specific problems in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Development versus production differences and Application pool configuration.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study debugging deployment-specific problems as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 91 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Debugging Deployment-Specific Problems matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Troubleshooting needs reproducible evidence. For 'Debugging Deployment-Specific Problems', distinguish parse/syntax failures, runtime failures, IIS configuration problems, dependency failures, and application logic defects. Capture a correlation identifier and useful server-side diagnostics; show visitors a stable, non-sensitive error message. Do not enable detailed ASP errors to the browser in production.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Development versus production differences; Application pool configuration; Filesystem access problems; Database driver problems; Server identity and permissions; Missing COM components; Differences in installed runtime dependencies. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Debugging Deployment-Specific Problems
content_blocks.code:
# Example only: inspect recent IIS logs via the configured log folder
Get-ChildItem "$env:SystemDrive\inetpub\logs\LogFiles" -Filter *.log -Recurse | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 FullName, LastWriteTime
content_blocks.expected_output: The newest IIS log files are listed (actual folders and permissions vary).
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use the correct IIS site log directory; protect logs and redact cookies, tokens, query-string secrets and personal data before sharing. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use an authorized local copy and benign synthetic data. Verify the expected denial/error path as well as the permitted path; never expose real secrets in examples or logs. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of debugging deployment-specific problems. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of debugging deployment-specific problems using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Development versus production differences. State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

task: Build a short demonstration of debugging deployment-specific problems using synthetic data. Demonstrate “Development versus production differences”, state the expected result, and document one edge/failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The artifact demonstrates Development versus production differences.
Expected result is written before verification.
At least one invalid or boundary case is documented.
Runtime/provider/version assumptions and security limits are recorded.

Keep the sample synthetic and change one thing at a time.

The syllabus coverage includes Development versus production differences; Application pool configuration; Filesystem access problems; Database driver problems; Server identity and permissions; Missing COM components; Differences in installed runtime dependencies.
A reproducible legacy-code example records input, environment/version, expected outcome, observed outcome, and a meaningful failure case.
expected_output: The newest IIS log files are listed (actual folders and permissions vary).

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
